techniques.name: Demographic Parity Assessment
techniques.description: Demographic Parity Assessment checks whether a model gives a favourable outcome, such as a loan approval or an interview invitation, to each demographic group at the same rate. It compares those rates without adjusting for how many people in each group would qualify. Statistical Parity Difference is the gap between group rates (a signed difference between two named groups in AIF360, the highest rate minus the lowest across all groups in Fairlearn), and the Disparate Impact ratio divides the lowest rate by the highest. A ratio below 0.8 is a common warning sign, following the four-fifths rule used by US employment regulators. A gap shows that outcomes differ between groups but not why, and equal rates do not show that individuals were treated fairly.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model risk team compares loan approval rates for applicants of different ethnic groups in the validation sample before a credit model goes live. It reports the ratio of the lowest to the highest approval rate and checks it against the 0.8 rule of thumb from US employment practice, treating a lower ratio as a prompt to investigate rather than a verdict.

An employer's HR analytics team tracks each month the share of male and female applicants that a CV-screening tool passes to interview. A widening gap in pass rates triggers a review of the tool before the next hiring round, even where the two applicant pools differ.

A local council checks whether its automated screening tool refers benefit claims for fraud investigation at similar rates across ethnic groups. Because a referral is a burden rather than a benefit, a higher referral rate for one group is a red flag that officers then examine case by case.

limitations.description: Parity can be met by unfair selection. A model can match approval rates by choosing less suitable applicants from one group, and the metric looks only at outcome rates, so it cannot tell. Dwork et al. give this as a standard example of why parity alone is not enough.

May penalise a model for real differences between groups in how many members qualify (the base rate), such as differing clinical need by age, and so push towards artificial equality where none should exist.
Can conflict with individual fairness principles, where similarly qualified individuals might receive different treatment to achieve group parity.

A pass on one attribute can hide large gaps inside subgroups, such as older women within a comparison by gender. The common 0.8 ratio threshold is a rule of thumb from US employment practice, so passing it is a screen rather than evidence of compliance in other domains.
A rate ratio depends on which group is the reference and can be unstable when its positive rate is very small. It is undefined when the denominator rate is zero.

resources.title: Fairness Through Awareness
resources.abstract: We study fairness in classification, where individuals are classified, e.g., admitted to a university, and the goal is to prevent discrimination against individuals based on their membership in some group, while maintaining utility for the classifier (the university). The main conceptual contribution of this paper is a framework for fair classification comprising (1) a (hypothetical) task-specific metric for determining the degree to which individuals are similar with respect to the classification task at hand; (2) an algorithm for maximizing utility subject to the fairness constraint, that similar individuals are treated similarly. We also present an adaptation of our approach to achieve the complementary goal of "fair affirmative action," which guarantees statistical parity (i.e., the demographics of the set of individuals receiving any classification are the same as the demographics of the underlying population), while treating similar individuals as similarly as possible. Finally, we discuss the relationship of fairness to privacy: when fairness implies privacy, and how tools developed in the context of differential privacy may be applied to fairness.

resources.title: Certifying and Removing Disparate Impact
resources.abstract: What does it mean for an algorithm to be biased? In U.S. law, unintentional bias is encoded via disparate impact, which occurs when a selection process has widely different outcomes for different groups, even as it appears to be neutral. This legal determination hinges on a definition of a protected class (ethnicity, gender) and an explicit description of the process. When computers are involved, determining disparate impact (and hence bias) is harder. It might not be possible to disclose the process. In addition, even if the process is open, it might be hard to elucidate in a legal setting how the algorithm makes its decisions. Instead of requiring access to the process, we propose making inferences based on the data it uses. We present four contributions. First, we link disparate impact to a measure of classification accuracy that while known, has received relatively little attention. Second, we propose a test for disparate impact based on how well the protected class can be predicted from the other attributes. Third, we describe methods by which data might be made unbiased. Finally, we present empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of our test for disparate impact and our approach for both masking bias and preserving relevant information in the data. Interestingly, our approach resembles some actual selection practices that have recently received legal scrutiny.

resources.title: A Data-Centric Approach to Detecting and Mitigating Demographic Bias in Pediatric Mental Health Text: A Case Study in Anxiety Detection
resources.abstract: Introduction: Healthcare AI models often inherit biases from their training data. While efforts have primarily targeted bias in structured data, mental health heavily depends on unstructured data. This study aims to detect and mitigate linguistic differences related to non-biological differences in the training data of AI models designed to assist in pediatric mental health screening. Our objectives are: (1) to assess the presence of bias by evaluating outcome parity across sex subgroups, (2) to identify bias sources through textual distribution analysis, and (3) to develop a de-biasing method for mental health text data. Methods: We examined classification parity across demographic groups and assessed how gendered language influences model predictions. A data-centric de-biasing method was applied, focusing on neutralizing biased terms while retaining salient clinical information. This methodology was tested on a model for automatic anxiety detection in pediatric patients. Results: Our findings revealed a systematic under-diagnosis of female adolescent patients, with a 4% lower accuracy and a 9% higher False Negative Rate (FNR) compared to male patients, likely due to disparities in information density and linguistic differences in patient notes. Notes for male patients were on average 500 words longer, and linguistic similarity metrics indicated distinct word distributions between genders. Implementing our de-biasing approach reduced diagnostic bias by up to 27%, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing equity across demographic groups. Discussion: We developed a data-centric de-biasing framework to address gender-based content disparities within clinical text. By neutralizing biased language and enhancing focus on clinically essential information, our approach demonstrates an effective strategy for mitigating bias in AI healthcare models trained on text.

resources.title: An empirical characterization of fair machine learning for clinical risk prediction
resources.abstract: The use of machine learning to guide clinical decision making has the potential to worsen existing health disparities. Several recent works frame the problem as that of algorithmic fairness, a framework that has attracted considerable attention and criticism. However, the appropriateness of this framework is unclear due to both ethical as well as technical considerations, the latter of which include trade-offs between measures of fairness and model performance that are not well-understood for predictive models of clinical outcomes. To inform the ongoing debate, we conduct an empirical study to characterize the impact of penalizing group fairness violations on an array of measures of model performance and group fairness. We repeat the analysis across multiple observational healthcare databases, clinical outcomes, and sensitive attributes. We find that procedures that penalize differences between the distributions of predictions across groups induce nearly-universal degradation of multiple performance metrics within groups. On examining the secondary impact of these procedures, we observe heterogeneity of the effect of these procedures on measures of fairness in calibration and ranking across experimental conditions. Beyond the reported trade-offs, we emphasize that analyses of algorithmic fairness in healthcare lack the contextual grounding and causal awareness necessary to reason about the mechanisms that lead to health disparities, as well as about the potential of algorithmic fairness methods to counteract those mechanisms. In light of these limitations, we encourage researchers building predictive models for clinical use to step outside the algorithmic fairness frame and engage critically with the broader sociotechnical context surrounding the use of machine learning in healthcare.

techniques.name: Adversarial Debiasing
techniques.description: Adversarial debiasing trains a model so that its predictions carry as little information as possible about a protected attribute, such as sex or race. Two neural networks are trained together, a predictor that learns the main task, such as estimating default risk, and an adversary that tries to guess each person's protected attribute from the predictor's output. The predictor is updated to stay accurate while making the adversary's guesses fail, which pushes its outputs towards equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups (demographic parity). If the adversary is also given the true label, the predictor is penalised only for information about the attribute beyond what the label carries, which targets equal error rates across groups (equalised odds). The method needs the protected attribute for every training example and a model trained by gradient descent.

example_use_cases.description: A technology company trains a CV-screening model with an adversary that tries to guess each applicant's gender from the model's shortlisting score, so that selection rates come out similar for men and women (demographic parity) instead of leaning on CV features that happen to correlate with gender.

A lender trains a default-risk model for loan approvals with an adversary that is given each applicant's score and true repayment outcome and tries to guess their age band, so that false-positive and false-negative rates are similar across age bands (equalised odds) while predictive accuracy is kept.

A hospital group trains a COVID-19 screening model on emergency-department data with an adversary that tries to guess patient ethnicity from the model's score and the true test result, so that error rates are similar across ethnic groups while screening performance stays clinically useful.

limitations.description: The adversary only sees what it is given, usually the predictor's score and, for equalised odds, the true label. The method therefore targets one output-level criterion and gives no assurance that hidden layers are free of protected-attribute information, or that a different criterion holds.
Needs the protected attribute for every training example, so it cannot be used where that attribute was never collected or may not be held.

Demographic parity and equalised odds generally cannot both be met, so one must be chosen before training. Equal error rates can also come from worsening one group's rates: in the original Adult income experiment, the false-positive rate for women rose from 0.025 to 0.065.

Training two networks against each other is unstable. The weight given to the adversary has to be tuned (adversary_loss_weight in AIF360), and a wrong setting can make training diverge or leave the result closer to a different criterion than the one intended.

The paper's guarantee that outputs meet the chosen criterion holds only if both networks converge and the adversary is strong enough. A weak adversary leaves bias in place, and the convexity assumptions behind the proof do not hold for typical neural networks, so fairness has to be checked on held-out data after training.

resources.title: On the Fairness ROAD: Robust Optimization for Adversarial Debiasing
resources.abstract: In the field of algorithmic fairness, significant attention has been put on group fairness criteria, such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Nevertheless, these objectives, measured as global averages, have raised concerns about persistent local disparities between sensitive groups. In this work, we address the problem of local fairness, which ensures that the predictor is unbiased not only in terms of expectations over the whole population, but also within any subregion of the feature space, unknown at training time. To enforce this objective, we introduce ROAD, a novel approach that leverages the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework within a fair adversarial learning objective, where an adversary tries to infer the sensitive attribute from the predictions. Using an instance-level re-weighting strategy, ROAD is designed to prioritize inputs that are likely to be locally unfair, i.e. where the adversary faces the least difficulty in reconstructing the sensitive attribute. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method: it achieves Pareto dominance with respect to local fairness and accuracy for a given global fairness level across three standard datasets, and also enhances fairness generalization under distribution shift.

resources.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is a tool for building models that accurately represent input training data. When undesired biases concerning demographic groups are in the training data, well-trained models will reflect those biases. We present a framework for mitigating such biases by including a variable for the group of interest and simultaneously learning a predictor and an adversary. The input to the network X, here text or census data, produces a prediction Y, such as an analogy completion or income bracket, while the adversary tries to model a protected variable Z, here gender or zip code. The objective is to maximize the predictor's ability to predict Y while minimizing the adversary's ability to predict Z. Applied to analogy completion, this method results in accurate predictions that exhibit less evidence of stereotyping Z. When applied to a classification task using the UCI Adult (Census) Dataset, it results in a predictive model that does not lose much accuracy while achieving very close to equality of odds (Hardt, et al., 2016). The method is flexible and applicable to multiple definitions of fairness as well as a wide range of gradient-based learning models, including both regression and classification tasks.

resources.title: An adversarial training framework for mitigating algorithmic biases in clinical machine learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is becoming increasingly prominent in healthcare. Although its benefits are clear, growing attention is being given to how these tools may exacerbate existing biases and disparities. In this study, we introduce an adversarial training framework that is capable of mitigating biases that may have been acquired through data collection. We demonstrate this proposed framework on the real-world task of rapidly predicting COVID-19, and focus on mitigating site-specific (hospital) and demographic (ethnicity) biases. Using the statistical definition of equalized odds, we show that adversarial training improves outcome fairness, while still achieving clinically-effective screening performances (negative predictive values >0.98). We compare our method to previous benchmarks, and perform prospective and external validation across four independent hospital cohorts. Our method can be generalized to any outcomes, models, and definitions of fairness.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance, and its accuracy is within the agreed margin of the unconstrained model.
The default-risk model's false-positive and false-negative rates differ between age bands by no more than the agreed tolerance on held-out data.
The COVID-19 screening model's error rates are similar across ethnic groups in each external hospital cohort, with negative predictive value above the clinical threshold set for screening.
Compared with the same model trained without the adversary, the model's gap on the chosen fairness criterion is smaller on held-out data, at a reported cost in accuracy.

techniques.name: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
techniques.description: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment tests whether a model would have made the same predictions for a person had their protected attribute, such as race or sex, been different, with everything that attribute influences changed accordingly (Kusner et al., 2017). The assessor first draws a causal graph, a diagram of which variables cause which, covering the protected attribute, the model's inputs and unobserved background factors, and fits it to data. For each person, the fitted graph is used to infer their background factors, switch the attribute to another value and recompute every input it influences, which gives a counterfactual version of that person. The model is run on both versions, and the gap between the two predictions, person by person or as a distance between the two sets of predictions, is the evidence for or against counterfactual fairness under the assumed graph. Every causal effect of the attribute counts as unfair, including effects passing through inputs such as test scores, which separates this criterion from versions that allow some pathways.

example_use_cases.description: A law school's admissions office uses a model to predict first-year grades from entrance-test scores and undergraduate grades. Its analysts build a causal model in which race and sex influence both inputs alongside an unobserved knowledge factor, fit it to past cohorts, and compare each applicant's predicted grade under actual and counterfactual race. A systematic shift shows that leaving race out of the inputs did not make the model counterfactually fair.

A credit risk team, working with economists, specifies a causal graph in which an applicant's ethnicity affects income and neighbourhood but not repayment behaviour directly, fits it to its applicant data, and checks whether the approval model's scores change for the counterfactual applicants. The result goes to the model risk committee together with the graph, because the conclusion holds only under that graph.

A public employment service reviewing a model that predicts job-seekers' risk of long-term unemployment from education and work history specifies, with labour-market researchers, how sex and migration background influence those inputs. It tests whether individual risk scores would change under counterfactual sex or migration background before the scores are used to allocate support.

limitations.description: The causal model can have testable implications, but its counterfactual assumptions are generally not identifiable from observed or experimental data. Plausible alternative models can therefore produce different fairness conclusions.

A common cause left out of the graph, such as school quality affecting both test scores and later grades, biases the counterfactuals without any warning sign. Kilbertus et al. (2019) show that counterfactual fairness is sensitive to such unmeasured confounding and give tools to bound the effect for additive noise models, which adds a further analysis to do.

Every effect of the attribute counts as unfair, so a model that uses an input the attribute influences will usually fail the test, unless those effects cancel out. Kusner et al. note that in practice few observed variables are unaffected by the attribute. Where some pathways are acceptable, for example where qualifications differ for reasons a decision may properly reflect, this criterion is stricter than the decision calls for.

Computing individual counterfactuals requires a fitted probabilistic model of the unobserved background factors; the original study fitted it in Stan, and DoWhy's counterfactual function needs mechanisms with additive noise and supports only continuous variables. With categorical inputs, many variables or unstructured data such as text and images, the assessment becomes hard to run or yields a spread of counterfactuals rather than one.

The counterfactual people are simulated by the fitted causal model, not observed. If its equations fit the data poorly or miss interactions, the counterfactual inputs are implausible and the measured gap reflects the causal model's errors as much as the predictor's; DoWhy's documentation notes counterfactual estimates are approximate for this reason.

resources.title: Counterfactual Fairness
resources.abstract: Machine learning can impact people with legal or ethical consequences when it is used to automate decisions in areas such as insurance, lending, hiring, and predictive policing. In many of these scenarios, previous decisions have been made that are unfairly biased against certain subpopulations, for example those of a particular race, gender, or sexual orientation. Since this past data may be biased, machine learning predictors must account for this to avoid perpetuating or creating discriminatory practices. In this paper, we develop a framework for modeling fairness using tools from causal inference. Our definition of counterfactual fairness captures the intuition that a decision is fair towards an individual if it the same in (a) the actual world and (b) a counterfactual world where the individual belonged to a different demographic group. We demonstrate our framework on a real-world problem of fair prediction of success in law school.

techniques.name: Causal Discrimination Testing
techniques.description: Causal discrimination testing checks whether a system gives different outputs to otherwise identical inputs because of a protected attribute, by changing only that attribute, or a name, term or other proxy that signals it, and measuring how often or how much the output changes. Galhotra, Brun and Meliou (2017), who called the approach fairness testing, generate inputs from a description of the valid input fields, make copies of each that differ only in the protected attribute (for example, recorded sex), run them all through the system as a black box, and report the causal discrimination score: the share of inputs whose decision changes, sampled until it is known within a chosen margin of error and confidence level. For text, the same test substitutes identity terms or names in otherwise unchanged sentences, such as one religion or ethnicity for another, and reports the average change in the model's score across the substitutions, which Garg et al. (2019) call the counterfactual token fairness gap. Because every other part of the input is held fixed, the test needs no model of how the attribute influences other variables: it measures whether the system itself responds to the attribute, or to the chosen proxy. The output is a score per attribute and, if the tester logs them, the input pairs whose outputs differed.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team tests a credit-approval model before release. For a sample of last year's applications it changes only the applicant's recorded sex, and separately their marital status, re-scores each pair, and reports the share of decisions that flip with a confidence interval, against a release threshold agreed with the compliance function.

A trust-and-safety team checks a toxicity classifier used to hold comments for review by substituting identity terms such as 'gay', 'Muslim' or 'Black' across a set of non-toxic comments. It measures the average change in toxicity score for each term and flags any term whose substitution pushes benign comments over the moderation threshold.

An HR technology supplier tests its CV-ranking service before a client deploys it, by submitting the same CVs under first names and surnames associated with different ethnicities and genders and reporting how often each candidate's rank or shortlisting changes.

A hospital's AI assurance lead tests a symptom-triage assistant with clinical vignettes that differ only in the patient's stated ethnicity. Clinicians first mark which vignettes should be unaffected by ethnicity, and only those pairs count as failures when the urgency rating changes.

limitations.description: Holding every other input fixed measures only the system's direct response to the attribute or proxy. It does not follow through the effects the attribute has on other inputs, such as career breaks on an employment history. Garg et al. note that token substitution is more limited than counterfactual fairness defined on a causal model. Where those downstream effects matter, a clean result does not show that individuals were treated fairly.

The test covers only what is perturbed. Unlisted identity terms, unperturbed proxies and multi-word references go undetected, as does discrimination that appears only when attributes change together: Galhotra et al. measured 11.2% for gender alone but 77.2% for gender, marital status and race together. Garg et al. found mitigation for listed terms generalised much less to held-out terms. A pass covers only the perturbations tried, and the list needs domain review.

Generated inputs may be unrealistic. Themis draws inputs uniformly from the input schema, so the score covers combinations that never occur in practice. Testing real inputs or an existing test suite avoids that, but the score is then only as representative as that set. Galhotra et al. note that Themis computes no confidence level for it, and an interval from a random sample of real cases covers sampling error only.

Not every substitution should leave the output unchanged. Garg et al. give 'That's so gay' versus 'That's so straight' as a pair a toxicity model may rightly score differently, and clinical risk can legitimately depend on sex. Without a judgement about which pairs must match, the test raises false alarms or, if such pairs are excluded wholesale, hides real failures.

A model can pass and still produce very different outcome or error rates across groups, because the test asks only whether changing the attribute changes the output, not whether outcomes are equal. Galhotra et al. distinguish this causal discrimination from group discrimination, and Garg et al. note that a text classifier can satisfy counterfactual fairness while completely failing equality of odds, so it does not replace group metrics.

resources.title: Fairness testing: testing software for discrimination
resources.abstract: This paper defines software fairness and discrimination and develops a testing-based method for measuring if and how much software discriminates, focusing on causality in discriminatory behavior. Evidence of software discrimination has been found in modern software systems that recommend criminal sentences, grant access to financial products, and determine who is allowed to participate in promotions. Our approach, Themis, generates efficient test suites to measure discrimination. Given a schema describing valid system inputs, Themis generates discrimination tests automatically and does not require an oracle. We evaluate Themis on 20 software systems, 12 of which come from prior work with explicit focus on avoiding discrimination. We find that (1) Themis is effective at discovering software discrimination, (2) state-of-the-art techniques for removing discrimination from algorithms fail in many situations, at times discriminating against as much as 98% of an input subdomain, (3) Themis optimizations are effective at producing efficient test suites for measuring discrimination, and (4) Themis is more efficient on systems that exhibit more discrimination. We thus demonstrate that fairness testing is a critical aspect of the software development cycle in domains with possible discrimination and provide initial tools for measuring software discrimination.

resources.title: BiasFinder: Metamorphic Test Generation to Uncover Bias for Sentiment Analysis Systems
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems, such as Sentiment Analysis (SA) systems, typically learn from large amounts of data that may reflect human bias. Consequently, such systems may exhibit unintended demographic bias against specific characteristics (e.g., gender, occupation, country-of-origin, etc.). Such bias manifests in an SA system when it predicts different sentiments for similar texts that differ only in the characteristic of individuals described. To automatically uncover bias in SA systems, this paper presents BiasFinder, an approach that can discover biased predictions in SA systems via metamorphic testing. A key feature of BiasFinder is the automatic curation of suitable templates from any given text inputs, using various Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to identify words that describe demographic characteristics. Next, BiasFinder generates new texts from these templates by mutating words associated with a class of a characteristic (e.g., gender-specific words such as female names, she, her). These texts are then used to tease out bias in an SA system. BiasFinder identifies a bias-uncovering test case (BTC) when an SA system predicts different sentiments for texts that differ only in words associated with a different class (e.g., male vs. female) of a target characteristic (e.g., gender). We evaluate BiasFinder on 10 SA systems and 2 large scale datasets, and the results show that BiasFinder can create more BTCs than two popular baselines. We also conduct an annotation study and find that human annotators consistently think that test cases generated by BiasFinder are more fluent than the two baselines.

resources.title: Counterfactual Fairness in Text Classification through Robustness
resources.abstract: In this paper, we study counterfactual fairness in text classification, which asks the question: How would the prediction change if the sensitive attribute referenced in the example were different? Toxicity classifiers demonstrate a counterfactual fairness issue by predicting that "Some people are gay" is toxic while "Some people are straight" is nontoxic. We offer a metric, counterfactual token fairness (CTF), for measuring this particular form of fairness in text classifiers, and describe its relationship with group fairness. Further, we offer three approaches, blindness, counterfactual augmentation, and counterfactual logit pairing (CLP), for optimizing counterfactual token fairness during training, bridging the robustness and fairness literature. Empirically, we find that blindness and CLP address counterfactual token fairness. The methods do not harm classifier performance, and have varying tradeoffs with group fairness. These approaches, both for measurement and optimization, provide a new path forward for addressing fairness concerns in text classification.

resources.title: Gender, Race, and Intersectional Bias in Resume Screening via Language Model Retrieval
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) hiring tools have revolutionized resume screening, and large language models (LLMs) have the potential to do the same. However, given the biases which are embedded within LLMs, it is unclear whether they can be used in this scenario without disadvantaging groups based on their protected attributes. In this work, we investigate the possibilities of using LLMs in a resume screening setting via a document retrieval framework that simulates job candidate selection. Using that framework, we then perform a resume audit study to determine whether a selection of Massive Text Embedding (MTE) models are biased in resume screening scenarios. We simulate this for nine occupations, using a collection of over 500 publicly available resumes and 500 job descriptions. We find that the MTEs are biased, significantly favoring White-associated names in 85.1% of cases and female-associated names in only 11.1% of cases, with a minority of cases showing no statistically significant differences. Further analyses show that Black males are disadvantaged in up to 100% of cases, replicating real-world patterns of bias in employment settings, and validate three hypotheses of intersectionality. We also find an impact of document length as well as the corpus frequency of names in the selection of resumes. These findings have implications for widely used AI tools that are automating employment, fairness, and tech policy.

techniques.name: Model Cards
techniques.description: A model card is a short structured document published with a trained model, stating what the model is for and what it should not be used for. It reports how the model performs on stated evaluation data, with results broken down by group (for example age or sex) and by operating condition (for example lighting or device) where these matter. It also records the training data, the metrics chosen and why, ethical considerations and known caveats. Readers use the card to judge whether the model suits their purpose before they deploy it. The original proposal gives suggested sections rather than a fixed format, and a card is only as reliable as the evaluation behind it.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical diagnosis AI with detailed performance metrics across different patient demographics, age groups, and clinical conditions, enabling healthcare providers to understand when the model should be trusted and when additional expert consultation is needed for patient safety.

Publishing a model card for a CV-screening model that reports selection rates and error rates for each gender and age band. An HR team deciding whether to adopt the tool can see where results differ between groups and ask the vendor for further evidence before using it.

Publishing detailed model documentation for a credit scoring API that clearly describes training data sources, evaluation methodologies, and performance limitations, enabling financial institutions to make informed decisions about model deployment and regulatory compliance.

A public body that buys AI tools asks each supplier for a model card and files it in its register of deployed models. Before approving a tool for a new use, officials compare the card's stated intended use and evaluation data with the proposed use and record any gaps.

limitations.description: Group-wise results need evaluation data labelled with the relevant attributes, which is often unavailable or restricted for privacy and legal reasons. Teams then report fewer groups than matter, and building the card takes time and statistical skill that can delay release.

Cards are written by the developer and nothing in the format requires an independent check. Unflattering results or commercially sensitive details can be left out, and a study of 32,111 Hugging Face model cards found the evaluation and limitations sections among the least often completed.

A card describes the model as evaluated at one point, on particular test data. Retraining, new deployment settings and data drift make it stale, and it stays in circulation unless someone owns updates and versioning.

A machine-readable model card format now exists (the model card object in the CycloneDX bill of materials, defined in ECMA-424, second edition, December 2025). The original template is still a set of suggested sections, and cards differ widely in structure and depth, which makes them hard to compare across models and vendors.

A card informs readers but does not constrain use or show that the model is safe. It cannot stop deployment outside the stated intended use, and the evidence it carries is only as good as the evaluations behind it.

resources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
resources.abstract: Trained machine learning models are increasingly used to perform high-impact tasks in areas such as law enforcement, medicine, education, and employment. In order to clarify the intended use cases of machine learning models and minimize their usage in contexts for which they are not well suited, we recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics. In this paper, we propose a framework that we call model cards, to encourage such transparent model reporting. Model cards are short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions, such as across different cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups (e.g., race, geographic location, sex, Fitzpatrick skin type) and intersectional groups (e.g., age and race, or sex and Fitzpatrick skin type) that are relevant to the intended application domains. Model cards also disclose the context in which models are intended to be used, details of the performance evaluation procedures, and other relevant information. While we focus primarily on human-centered machine learning models in the application fields of computer vision and natural language processing, this framework can be used to document any trained machine learning model. To solidify the concept, we provide cards for two supervised models: One trained to detect smiling faces in images, and one trained to detect toxic comments in text. We propose model cards as a step towards the responsible democratization of machine learning and related AI technology, increasing transparency into how well AI technology works. We hope this work encourages those releasing trained machine learning models to accompany model releases with similar detailed evaluation numbers and other relevant documentation.

resources.title: Systematic analysis of 32,111 AI model cards characterizes documentation practice in AI
Interactive Model Cards: A Human-Centered Approach to Model Documentation
resources.abstract: Deep learning models for natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly adopted and deployed by analysts without formal training in NLP or machine learning (ML). However, the documentation intended to convey the model’s details and appropriate use is tailored primarily to individuals with ML or NLP expertise. To address this gap, we conduct a design inquiry into interactive model cards, which augment traditionally static model cards with affordances for exploring model documentation and interacting with the models themselves. Our investigation consists of an initial conceptual study with experts in ML, NLP, and AI Ethics, followed by a separate evaluative study with non-expert analysts who use ML models in their work. Using a semi-structured interview format coupled with a think-aloud protocol, we collected feedback from a total of 30 participants who engaged with different versions of standard and interactive model cards. Through a thematic analysis of the collected data, we identified several conceptual dimensions that summarize the strengths and limitations of standard and interactive model cards, including: stakeholders; design; guidance; understandability & interpretability; sensemaking & skepticism; and trust & safety. Our findings demonstrate the importance of carefully considered design and interactivity for orienting and supporting non-expert analysts using deep learning models, along with a need for consideration of broader sociotechnical contexts and organizational dynamics. We have also identified design elements, such as language, visual cues, and warnings, among others, that support interactivity and make non-interactive content accessible. We summarize our findings as design guidelines and discuss their implications for a human-centered approach towards AI/ML documentation.

techniques.name: Reweighing
techniques.description: Reweighing is a fairness method, presented by Kamiran and Calders (2012), that adjusts the training data before any model is trained so that a protected attribute, such as sex or ethnicity, has no statistical link to the outcome label. It does this by giving each training example a weight, leaving every feature value and label unchanged. Each combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired) gets a weight equal to the number of examples it would hold if group and label were unrelated, divided by the number it actually holds. Combinations rarer than that expectation, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so every group has the same rate of positive labels in the weighted data. A model is then trained on the original data with these weights, so the learning algorithm must accept example weights.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model team finds that in the historical loan decisions used as training labels, applicants from one ethnic group were approved far less often than others. Before retraining its approval model it computes reweighing weights, so that approved applicants from that group count for more and refused ones for less, trains with them as sample weights, and compares the approval-rate gap and accuracy on held-out data against the unweighted model.

A health insurer's analytics team building a model to target postpartum depression outreach from Medicaid claims compares reweighing by race with simply removing race from the inputs. It reports each option's disparate impact ratio (the ratio of positive-prediction rates between groups) and predictive performance to its clinical governance group before choosing one.

A recruitment platform training a shortlisting model on past hiring outcomes, in which women were hired into senior engineering roles less often than men, applies reweighing by sex before training so that the weighted history shows equal hiring rates, then checks shortlisting rates by sex on a held-out set of applications.

limitations.description: Its target is fixed: equal rates of positive labels across groups in the weighted training data (statistical parity). It does not aim at equal error rates such as equal opportunity, and the weights are computed once, before training, so they cannot respond to where the trained model actually errs. An adaptive variant (Krasanakis et al., 2018) re-estimates weights during training for error-rate criteria, but it has no maintained implementation.

It removes all association between group and label, including any part a legitimate factor explains. Kamiran and Calders give the example of car insurance, where more accidents among men may justify different outcomes by sex; reweighing erases that difference too, so it over-corrects wherever some gap between groups is warranted.

The learning algorithm must accept example weights; where it cannot, the data have to be resampled instead, which is a different method. Only the training data are balanced, so the trained model's predictions are not guaranteed to be: outcome rates by group must be measured on held-out data after training rather than assumed.

When a group-label combination is rare its weight is large (a combination with a tenth of its expected count gets a weight of ten), so a handful of examples can dominate training. This raises variance and amplifies any labelling errors in exactly the group the method is meant to protect, and it bites hardest with small or intersectional groups.
An absent group-label combination cannot be created by weighting existing records. Zero observed counts require explicit handling rather than applying the ratio unchanged.

resources.title: Data preprocessing techniques for classification without discrimination
resources.abstract: Recently, the following Discrimination-Aware Classification Problem was introduced: Suppose we are given training data that exhibit unlawful discrimination; e.g., toward sensitive attributes such as gender or ethnicity. The task is to learn a classifier that optimizes accuracy, but does not have this discrimination in its predictions on test data. This problem is relevant in many settings, such as when the data are generated by a biased decision process or when the sensitive attribute serves as a proxy for unobserved features. In this paper, we concentrate on the case with only one binary sensitive attribute and a two-class classification problem. We first study the theoretically optimal trade-off between accuracy and non-discrimination for pure classifiers. Then, we look at algorithmic solutions that preprocess the data to remove discrimination before a classifier is learned. We survey and extend our existing data preprocessing techniques, being suppression of the sensitive attribute, massaging the dataset by changing class labels, and reweighing or resampling the data to remove discrimination without relabeling instances. These preprocessing techniques have been implemented in a modified version of Weka and we present the results of experiments on real-life data.

resources.title: Comparison of Methods to Reduce Bias From Clinical Prediction Models of Postpartum Depression
resources.abstract: Importance: The lack of standards in methods to reduce bias for clinical algorithms presents various challenges in providing reliable predictions and in addressing health disparities. Objective: To evaluate approaches for reducing bias in machine learning models using a real-world clinical scenario. Design, Setting, and Participants: Health data for this cohort study were obtained from the IBM MarketScan Medicaid Database. Eligibility criteria were as follows: (1) Female individuals aged 12 to 55 years with a live birth record identified by delivery-related codes from January 1, 2014, through December 31, 2018; (2) greater than 80% enrollment through pregnancy to 60 days post partum; and (3) evidence of coverage for depression screening and mental health services. Statistical analysis was performed in 2020. Exposures: Binarized race (Black individuals and White individuals). Main Outcomes and Measures: Machine learning models (logistic regression [LR], random forest, and extreme gradient boosting) were trained for 2 binary outcomes: postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum mental health service utilization. Risk-adjusted generalized linear models were used for each outcome to assess potential disparity in the cohort associated with binarized race (Black or White). Methods for reducing bias, including reweighing, Prejudice Remover, and removing race from the models, were examined by analyzing changes in fairness metrics compared with the base models. Baseline characteristics of female individuals at the top-predicted risk decile were compared for systematic differences. Fairness metrics of disparate impact (DI, 1 indicates fairness) and equal opportunity difference (EOD, 0 indicates fairness). Results: Among 573 634 female individuals initially examined for this study, 314 903 were White (54.9%), 217 899 were Black (38.0%), and the mean (SD) age was 26.1 (5.5) years. The risk-adjusted odds ratio comparing White participants with Black participants was 2.06 (95% CI, 2.02-2.10) for clinically recognized PPD and 1.37 (95% CI, 1.33-1.40) for postpartum mental health service utilization. Taking the LR model for PPD prediction as an example, reweighing reduced bias as measured by improved DI and EOD metrics from 0.31 and -0.19 to 0.79 and 0.02, respectively. Removing race from the models had inferior performance for reducing bias compared with the other methods (PPD: DI = 0.61; EOD = -0.05; mental health service utilization: DI = 0.63; EOD = -0.04). Conclusions and Relevance: Clinical prediction models trained on potentially biased data may produce unfair outcomes on the basis of the chosen metrics. This study's results suggest that the performance varied depending on the model, outcome label, and method for reducing bias. This approach toward evaluating algorithmic bias can be used as an example for the growing number of researchers who wish to examine and address bias in their data and models.

resources.title: Bias Discovery in Machine Learning Models for Mental Health
resources.abstract: Fairness and bias are crucial concepts in artificial intelligence, yet they are relatively ignored in machine learning applications in clinical psychiatry. We computed fairness metrics and present bias mitigation strategies using a model trained on clinical mental health data. We collected structured data related to the admission, diagnosis, and treatment of patients in the psychiatry department of the University Medical Center Utrecht. We trained a machine learning model to predict future administrations of benzodiazepines on the basis of past data. We found that gender plays an unexpected role in the predictions—this constitutes bias. Using the AI Fairness 360 package, we implemented reweighing and discrimination-aware regularization as bias mitigation strategies, and we explored their implications for model performance. This is the first application of bias exploration and mitigation in a machine learning model trained on real clinical psychiatry data.

techniques.name: Disparate Impact Remover
techniques.description: Disparate Impact Remover is a pre-processing method that edits the numerical features of a dataset so that they reveal less about a protected attribute such as race or sex. For each feature it compares how the values are distributed within each protected group, then moves every value towards a shared distribution while keeping its rank within its own group, so people near the top of their group stay near the top. The user sets a repair level from 0 (no change) to 1 (each feature is distributed identically in every group). The aim is to avoid disparate impact, where one group's selection rate falls below 80 per cent of the most favoured group's rate. Stronger repair narrows that gap but costs predictive accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's data science team finds that income, length of employment and credit history length in its loan dataset differ systematically between applicants under and over 25. It repairs those three features at a level of 0.8, trains its scoring model on the repaired data, and checks the approval-rate ratio between the age groups against the 80 per cent threshold to decide whether a stronger repair is needed.

A fire service reviewing a promotion process finds that written and oral exam scores differ between ethnic groups, so a 70 per cent pass mark selects far fewer candidates from one group. It repairs both scores while keeping each candidate's rank within their own group, then checks whether the repaired scores still separate stronger candidates from weaker ones.

limitations.description: Repair costs predictive accuracy, and the cost varies sharply by dataset. In the original experiments a full repair cut a measure of classifier utility on the German credit data from about 72 per cent to about 50 per cent, close to chance, but the Adult income data lost only about two points. The repair level has to be chosen and justified.

It repairs numerical features only, and the AIF360 implementation takes one protected attribute at a time. Categorical features such as job title or postcode are left unchanged and can still carry the protected attribute, and repairing several attributes together means the user must define the joint groups.

Each feature is repaired separately, so every feature can look identical across groups while combinations of features still reveal the protected attribute. A model trained on several repaired features may therefore still show disparate impact, which is why the original paper pairs the repair with a test that tries to predict the protected attribute from all the features together.

The repair depends on each person's protected attribute and on the group distributions seen in the training data. AIF360 notes that new data can be transformed the same way only if those conditional distributions match, and each new record needs its protected attribute, which makes the method awkward for a live scoring service.

The target is the US 80 per cent rule, a comparison of group selection rates, and the paper notes that other legal frameworks may need a different formulation. The rule says nothing about how individuals are treated, and the paper points out that disparate impact is not itself unlawful where a business necessity can be shown.

resources.title: Certifying and Removing Disparate Impact
resources.abstract: What does it mean for an algorithm to be biased? In U.S. law, unintentional bias is encoded via disparate impact, which occurs when a selection process has widely different outcomes for different groups, even as it appears to be neutral. This legal determination hinges on a definition of a protected class (ethnicity, gender) and an explicit description of the process. When computers are involved, determining disparate impact (and hence bias) is harder. It might not be possible to disclose the process. In addition, even if the process is open, it might be hard to elucidate in a legal setting how the algorithm makes its decisions. Instead of requiring access to the process, we propose making inferences based on the data it uses. We present four contributions. First, we link disparate impact to a measure of classification accuracy that while known, has received relatively little attention. Second, we propose a test for disparate impact based on how well the protected class can be predicted from the other attributes. Third, we describe methods by which data might be made unbiased. Finally, we present empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of our test for disparate impact and our approach for both masking bias and preserving relevant information in the data. Interestingly, our approach resembles some actual selection practices that have recently received legal scrutiny.

resources.title: A comparative study of fairness-enhancing interventions in machine learning
resources.abstract: Computers are increasingly used to make decisions that have significant impact on people's lives. Often, these predictions can affect different population subgroups disproportionately. As a result, the issue of fairness has received much recent interest, and a number of fairness-enhanced classifiers have appeared in the literature. This paper seeks to study the following questions: how do these different techniques fundamentally compare to one another, and what accounts for the differences? Specifically, we seek to bring attention to many under-appreciated aspects of such fairness-enhancing interventions that require investigation for these algorithms to receive broad adoption.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

The loss in predictive accuracy caused by the repair is documented and stays within the tolerance agreed with the credit risk team.

techniques.name: Fairness GAN
techniques.description: Fairness GAN is a pre-processing method that generates a synthetic training dataset in which decisions no longer track a protected attribute such as gender or skin tone. A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a pair of networks trained against each other, one producing fake examples and one trying to tell them from real ones. Here the generator is conditioned on the protected attribute and produces both an example and its decision label, such as hired or rejected (images in the original work, table rows in Xu et al.'s separate FairGAN). An extra network tries to predict the protected attribute from the generated output, and the generator is rewarded for defeating it, so favourable decisions become more similar across groups. The user can aim for demographic parity, meaning equal rates of favourable decisions, or for equality of opportunity, which applies the constraint only to favourable decisions.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment technology team holds interview-video stills labelled with past shortlisting decisions that favoured one gender. It trains a Fairness GAN to generate a synthetic image set whose shortlisting labels are similar for women and men, trains the screening model on that set, and compares shortlisting rates by gender on held-out real images before deployment.

A lender's data science team has ten years of loan decisions in which women were approved less often than men on similar incomes. It trains a tabular FairGAN-style generator to produce a synthetic dataset, confirms that the gap in approval rates in the synthetic data is close to zero, and trains its scoring model on that data, testing accuracy and approval rates on real held-out applications.

limitations.description: GAN training is unstable and the fairness loss adds a further pull on the generator. The original authors used spectral normalisation, softened outcome values and added noise to keep training stable, and results still varied across datasets. Expect tuning effort and repeated runs.

Fairness and accuracy trade off, and the gain is uneven. In the original experiments a classifier trained on debiased CelebA data went from about 20 to about 29 per cent error. Demographic parity improved on three of four datasets but not on Quick, Draw!, and the demographic-parity version made equality of opportunity worse on the soccer data.

It needs a lot of data. The authors had only 1,501 labelled soccer images, so they borrowed more than 200,000 unlabelled CelebA faces to help the generator, which is possible only when a large related set exists.

The original method covers a narrow setting: image inputs, one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome, with demographic parity or equality of opportunity but not equalised odds. Continuous protected attributes and non-image data are left as future work, and tabular versions such as FairGAN are separate methods with their own evidence.

Fairness is judged by training a classifier on the synthetic data and testing it on real data, and image quality is judged mainly by inspecting average faces. The authors report that debiasing visibly changes images in stereotyped ways, such as male faces taking on features coded as feminine, so the synthetic data need checking for distortions that the classifier test would miss.

resources.title: Fairness GAN
resources.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Fairness GAN, an approach for generating a dataset that is plausibly similar to a given multimedia dataset, but is more fair with respect to protected attributes in allocative decision making. We propose a novel auxiliary classifier GAN that strives for demographic parity or equality of opportunity and show empirical results on several datasets, including the CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA) dataset, the Quick, Draw!\ dataset, and a dataset of soccer player images and the offenses they were called for. The proposed formulation is well-suited to absorbing unlabeled data; we leverage this to augment the soccer dataset with the much larger CelebA dataset. The methodology tends to improve demographic parity and equality of opportunity while generating plausible images.

resources.title: FairGAN: Fairness-aware Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Fairness-aware learning is increasingly important in data mining. Discrimination prevention aims to prevent discrimination in the training data before it is used to conduct predictive analysis. In this paper, we focus on fair data generation that ensures the generated data is discrimination free. Inspired by generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present fairness-aware generative adversarial networks, called FairGAN, which are able to learn a generator producing fair data and also preserving good data utility. Compared with the naive fair data generation models, FairGAN further ensures the classifiers which are trained on generated data can achieve fair classification on real data. Experiments on a real dataset show the effectiveness of FairGAN.

resources.title: Bt-GAN: Generating Fair Synthetic Healthdata via Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Synthetic data generation offers a promising solution to enhance the usefulness of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) by generating realistic de-identified data. However, the existing literature primarily focuses on the quality of synthetic health data, neglecting the crucial aspect of fairness in downstream predictions. Consequently, models trained on synthetic EHR have faced criticism for producing biased outcomes in target tasks. These biases can arise from either spurious correlations between features or the failure of models to accurately represent sub-groups. To address these concerns, we present Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks (Bt-GAN), a GAN-based synthetic data generator specifically designed for the healthcare domain. In order to tackle spurious correlations (i), we propose an information-constrained Data Generation Process (DGP) that enables the generator to learn a fair deterministic transformation based on a well-defined notion of algorithmic fairness. To overcome the challenge of capturing exact sub-group representations (ii), we incentivize the generator to preserve sub-group densities through score-based weighted sampling. This approach compels the generator to learn from underrepresented regions of the data manifold. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Our results demonstrate that Bt-GAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving fairness and minimizing bias amplification. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth explainability analysis to provide additional evidence supporting the validity of our study. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel and professional approach to addressing the limitations of synthetic data generation in the healthcare domain. By incorporating fairness considerations and leveraging advanced techniques such as GANs, we pave the way for more reliable and unbiased predictions in healthcare applications.

resources.title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-Aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
resources.abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

sample_claims.text: In the synthetic training set generated for the screening model, the rate of favourable shortlisting decisions for women and men differs by less than the tolerance set in the project's fairness requirement.
A credit scoring model trained on the synthetic loan data shows a smaller gap in approval rates between women and men, on held-out real applications, than a model trained on the original data.
The synthetic data remain close enough to the original for the model's purpose: the accuracy cost of training on them, compared with the original data, was measured and judged acceptable.

techniques.name: Relabelling
techniques.description: Relabelling, also called data massaging, is a pre-processing method proposed by Kamiran and Calders. It changes some of the outcome labels in a training set so that a protected group and everyone else have the same rate of positive outcomes, such as being hired or approved. A ranking model first scores each example by how likely it is to be positive. The method then promotes the highest-scoring negative examples from the disadvantaged group to positive and demotes the lowest-scoring positive examples from the favoured group to negative, in equal numbers. Because the examples closest to the decision boundary change first and the numbers are equal, the overall share of positive labels stays the same and the number of changes is as small as it can be.

example_use_cases.description: A public-sector recruiter's ten years of shortlisting records show women shortlisted less often than men with comparable applications. Before training a screening model, the data team flips the labels of the rejected women a ranking model scores highest and the shortlisted men it scores lowest, in equal numbers, until shortlisting rates match and the overall shortlisting rate is unchanged.

A building society finds that past loan decisions approved applicants from one ethnic minority far less often than others with similar finances, and suspects the gap reflects past discretion rather than risk. It flips borderline decisions in both directions, keeping the overall approval rate fixed, and trains its scoring model on the corrected labels while keeping the original labels in a separate file.

limitations.description: It assumes the whole gap in positive rates between groups is discrimination. The number of labels changed is set to bring the gap to zero, even where part of the gap has a legitimate explanation, and the original authors note that such constraints are often too strong.

It rewrites the record of what happened. The flipped labels no longer match the real decisions or outcomes, so it suits labels that record biased past decisions and is dangerous where labels are measured facts, such as a confirmed diagnosis or a repayment. The authors call the approach intrusive.

Which records are flipped depends on a ranking model trained on the same biased data. A poor ranker flips the wrong people, and in the original experiments the discrimination and accuracy of the final classifier varied with the learner trained afterwards.

It handles one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome. Gender and ethnicity together, or a numeric attribute such as income, are not covered, so correcting one attribute can leave intersectional gaps.

Accuracy falls as discrimination falls, and the authors prove the trade-off cannot be avoided. Discrimination is removed from the training data, but a model trained on it can still show some on new data.

The task is to learn a classifier that optimizes accuracy, but does not have this discrimination in its predictions on test data. This problem is relevant in many settings, such as when the data are generated by a biased decision process or when the sensitive attribute serves as a proxy for unobserved features. In this paper, we concentrate on the case with only one binary sensitive attribute and a two-class classification problem. We first study the theoretically optimal trade-off between accuracy and non-discrimination for pure classifiers. Then, we look at algorithmic solutions that preprocess the data to remove discrimination before a classifier is learned. We survey and extend our existing data preprocessing techniques, being suppression of the sensitive attribute, massaging the dataset by changing class labels, and reweighing or resampling the data to remove discrimination without relabeling instances. resources.title: Classifying without discriminating
resources.abstract: Classification models usually make predictions on the basis of training data. If the training data is biased towards certain groups or classes of objects, e.g., there is racial discrimination towards black people, the learned model will also show discriminatory behavior towards that particular community. This partial attitude of the learned model may lead to biased outcomes when labeling future unlabeled data objects. Often, however, impartial classification results are desired or even required by law for future data objects in spite of having biased training data. In this paper, we tackle this problem by introducing a new classification scheme for learning unbiased models on biased training data. Our method is based on massaging the dataset by making the least intrusive modifications which lead to an unbiased dataset. On this modified dataset we then learn a non-discriminating classifier. The proposed method has been implemented and experimental results on a credit approval dataset show promising results: in all experiments our method is able to reduce the prejudicial behavior for future classification significantly without loosing too much predictive accuracy.

sample_claims.text: In the corrected training set the share of positive labels is the same for women and men, and the overall share of positive labels is unchanged from the original data.
Only borderline cases, the examples nearest the ranking model's decision boundary, had their labels changed, in equal numbers in each direction, and no feature values were altered.
The lending model trained on the corrected labels shows a smaller gap in approval rates between age groups on held-out data than a model trained on the original labels.

techniques.name: Preferential Sampling
techniques.description: Preferential Sampling is a pre-processing method, proposed by Kamiran and Calders, that rebalances a training set so that a protected group and everyone else have the same rate of positive outcomes, such as being hired or approved. A ranking model first scores every example by how likely it is to have a positive label. The method then compares the size of each group-and-outcome combination with the size it would have if group and outcome were unrelated. It adds copies of positive examples from the disadvantaged group and negative examples from the favoured group, and removes negative examples from the disadvantaged group and positive examples from the favoured group, always starting with those closest to the decision boundary. Labels are never changed, so a standard classifier can learn from the rebalanced set.

example_use_cases.description: A graduate recruiter's historical shortlisting data shows women were shortlisted less often than men with similar scores. The team trains a ranking model, then copies the shortlisted women and rejected men closest to the decision boundary and removes the rejected women and shortlisted men closest to it, until the shortlisting rates match. No label is changed, and the production model is trained on the resampled set.

A bank training a loan-approval model on ten years of decisions finds that applicants under 25 were approved far less often than older applicants. Compliance wants the recorded decisions left untouched, so the model team resamples the training set until approval rates match across age groups and keeps the original labels as the record of what was decided.

limitations.description: Duplicating examples invites overfitting, and removing them discards information. The method copies the same borderline examples and drops others, so a model may memorise duplicates or lose cases it needed, which matters most when the training set is small or many changes are needed.

It assumes the whole gap in positive rates between groups is discrimination. It resamples until outcome and group are unrelated, even where part of the gap has a legitimate explanation such as differing experience, and the original authors note that this constraint is often too strong.

The result depends on a ranking model learned from the same biased data. The ranker decides which examples count as borderline, so a weak or biased ranker copies and removes the wrong ones, and in the original experiments the method worked best with unstable learners such as decision trees.

It handles one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome. Gender and ethnicity together are not covered, so resampling for one attribute can leave intersectional groups unbalanced, and the authors call multiple combined attributes a harder open problem.

Fairness is achieved on the training data, not guaranteed on new data. In the original Census Income experiment with decision trees, discrimination fell from about 16 to about 3 per cent, not to zero, and the protected attribute must be recorded for every training example.

resources.title: Data preprocessing techniques for classification without discrimination
resources.abstract: Recently, the following Discrimination-Aware Classification Problem was introduced: Suppose we are given training data that exhibit unlawful discrimination; e.g., toward sensitive attributes such as gender or ethnicity. The task is to learn a classifier that optimizes accuracy, but does not have this discrimination in its predictions on test data. This problem is relevant in many settings, such as when the data are generated by a biased decision process or when the sensitive attribute serves as a proxy for unobserved features. In this paper, we concentrate on the case with only one binary sensitive attribute and a two-class classification problem. We first study the theoretically optimal trade-off between accuracy and non-discrimination for pure classifiers. Then, we look at algorithmic solutions that preprocess the data to remove discrimination before a classifier is learned. We survey and extend our existing data preprocessing techniques, being suppression of the sensitive attribute, massaging the dataset by changing class labels, and reweighing or resampling the data to remove discrimination without relabeling instances. These preprocessing techniques have been implemented in a modified version of Weka and we present the results of experiments on real-life data.
